```{r message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
birthdays = function(n) {
  
  days = sample(x = 1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  
  anyDuplicated(days) > 0
  
}
```

```{r}
bday_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    sample_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    shared_bdays = map_lgl(sample_size, birthdays)
  )
```

```{r}
bday_prob_df = 
bday_results_df |> 
  group_by(sample_size) |> 
  summarize(
    shared_prob = mean(shared_bdays)
    ) 
```

```{r}
bday_prob_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_size, y = shared_prob)) + 
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Birthday Repeats by Sample Size", 
    x = "Sample Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday") 
```

There is a very low probability of shared birthdays when pulling a two person sample, and near 1 probability when pulling from a sample of 50. I was honestly surprised by this result -- I didn't expect the probability to be almost 100% at such a low sample size. The curve generally follows an S shape, with the largest slope in the middle range of the sample sizes. 

## Problem 2

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
longit_df = 
  tibble(files = list.files("data/")) |>
  mutate(
    path = str_c("data/", files),
    data = map(path, read_csv)
  ) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observed_value"
  ) |>
  mutate(subject = str_remove(files, ".csv")) |>
  separate(files, into = c("arm", "id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    id = str_remove(id, ".csv"),
    week = as.numeric(week)
  ) |>
  select(-path)
```

```{r}
longit_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observed_value, group = subject, color = arm)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Observed Values Over Time by Subject",
    x = "Time (weeks)",
    y = "Observed Value")
```

The experimental group generally displayed increasing observed values over time compared to the control, however each group had relatively similar baseline values. This is indicative that the experimental group was differentially impacted by treatment as compared to the control group. 

## Problem 3

```{r}
sim_ttest = function(n, mu = 0, sigma = 5) {

    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  
    t.test(x) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}
```

```{r}
sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    estimate_df = map(mu, \(mu) sim_ttest(n = 30, mu = mu))
  ) |> 
  unnest(estimate_df)
```

Plot for effect size and power (null rejection)

```{r}
sim_results_df |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05) |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(power = mean(rejected)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "True Values of mu versus Power",
    x = "True Value of mu",
    y = "Power"
  )
```

As effect size (mu) increases, power also increases. This means that the null is more frequently rejected at higher means. At mu = 0 the power is about 0.05, which means that even when the null is true the test will still reject 5% of the time.

Overlaid sample mean plots

```{r}
sim_results_df |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05) |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    avg_est = mean(estimate),
    avg_rej = mean(estimate[rejected])
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = avg_est, color = "All Samples")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = avg_est, color = "All Samples")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = avg_rej, color = "Null Rejected")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = avg_rej, color = "Null Rejected")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimate of mu versus True Value of mu",
    x = "True Value of mu",
    y = "Average Estimate of mu",
    color = "Sample Type"
  )
```

As the true values of mu increase, the average estimates of mu also increase generally. Lower true values of mu lead to higher average mu estimates in null rejected estimates compared to all estimates. Sample averages across tests when the null is rejected are approximately equal to the true value of mu from 4 to 6, however there is slight divergence at lower values due to a smaller power.
